claims.text: Attach a bar to the low pulley, take an underhand (palms-up) grip about shoulder-width apart, and step back from the stack.

quotes.text: Fasten a bar in the lower position of a cable cross. Grip the bar with an underhand (supinated) grip, hands about shoulder-width apart, and take a step back.

claims.text: Stand upright with the feet about hip-width apart, palms facing up.

quotes.text: Stand upright with your feet hip width apart while grabbing the handle so that your palms are facing up.

claims.text: Curl the bar toward the shoulders by bending the elbows, with the elbows kept close to the torso; the upper arms stay still or move only slightly forward, never back.

quotes.text: Don’t let your upper arm travel back during the curl, keep it still or move it slightly forward.
Bend your elbows to raise the handle up towards your shoulders keeping your elbows close your torso.

claims.text: Lift with control and return to the start under control.

quotes.text: Lift the bar with control, by flexing your elbows.
Controllably return to the starting position.

claims.text: Because the cable pulls at a slight diagonal, the arm flexors find it harder to relax than in a barbell curl, and the cable keeps tension near the top of the range.

quotes.text: Because the direction of pull is slightly diagonal to the ground, it is harder for the arm flexors to relax in this exercise.
This is especially helpful for applying tension at the top of your range of motion.

claims.text: StrengthLog lists the biceps as the primary muscle and the forearm flexors as secondary; the brachioradialis, a forearm muscle, also bends the elbow.

quotes.text: Primary muscles worked: Biceps Secondary muscles worked: Forearm Flexors
Biceps brachii is a robust forearm supinator and an elbow flexor while brachioradialis, the most superficial muscle of the forearm considering the radial part, acts as an elbow flexor

claims.text: Inferred from the dumbbell curl (same elbow action): elbows moving forward during the lift shift load to the front delts, and elbows moving back let you cheat the weight up.

quotes.text: If your elbows move forward while you’re lifting the weight, it will put an additional load on your front delts, instead of focusing on your biceps. If your elbows move backward, you’ll also move the load from your biceps and be able to “cheat up” the weight.

claims.text: Inferred from the dumbbell curl: swinging the body is the sign of a load that is too heavy; the fix is less weight and a controlled lift, with the body still and only the arms moving.

quotes.text: If you start to swing, you should probably remove some weight instead and focus on performing the movement with control.
Make sure to keep your elbows close to the body the entire time. Your body shouldn’t move, just the arms.

claims.text: Inferred from the dumbbell curl: keep the wrists straight; bent wrists add load to them and can cause discomfort.

quotes.text: Maintain a neutral wrist position (avoid flexion and extension of your wrists)
Keep your wrists straight during the movement. If they’re bent, it can put an unnecessary load on them and lead to discomfort and maybe even injuries.
quotes.where: Common mistakes, not locking your wrists

claims.text: Tempo (up = lifting, down = lowering): about 1 s up and 2 s down, inside ACSM's moderate speed of 1-2 s each way.

quotes.text: at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)

claims.text: Load progression: add 2-10% load once you can do one or two reps more than the target number.

quotes.text: When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

claims.text: In a 10-week study of unilateral cable curls, training with the shoulder neutral or maximally extended gave similar elbow-flexor growth when effort and range were matched.

quotes.text: altering shoulder extension angle in isolation does not appear to produce meaningful differences in elbow flexor hypertrophy in untrained men over 10 weeks.

claims.text: Fitbod calls losing tension at the bottom, with the arms fully extended, very common; the fix is to limit the range and keep the arm slightly bent between reps to maintain tension in the biceps.

quotes.text: It’s very common to lose tension at the bottom of the movement when your arms are fully extended. Limit your range of motion and keep your arm slightly bent to maintain tension in your biceps between reps.
quotes.where: Common mistakes, limit range of motion at the bottom

plate.viewWhy: Elbow bending runs front-to-back, so the elbow angle, including the slight bend at the bottom (c13), elbow drift (c3, c7) and body swing (c8) read side-on. Census view is side.
plate.equipment: Cable column with the pulley at the lowest position and a straight bar (c1); the lifter stands a step back from the stack on the floor line.
plate.start: Standing upright, feet about hip-width (c2), a step back from the low pulley (c1); arms down with the elbows slightly bent, not fully extended (c13), palms up on the bar, hands about shoulder-width (c1); elbows close to the torso (c3); wrists straight (c9).
plate.end: Elbows fully bent, bar near the shoulders (c3); upper arms still or slightly forward, never back (c3); body in the same upright position (c8); wrists straight (c9).

rows.fix: Keep the elbows at your sides.
